opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most interesting parts of that line of work, and honestly one of the parts we understand least.

Some context first. When we meta-learn or discover objective functions, whether it's the drift function in Learned Policy Optimization or the preference losses the LLM proposed in the DiscoPOP work, we get back a function that does well empirically. Then we plot it and stare at it. A lot of what you see makes sense in hindsight. You get something like a rollback or clipping behavior far from the current policy, which is roughly what PPO hand-engineers. But right around the origin, where the advantage is near zero and you've barely moved from the reference or behavior policy, you sometimes get these odd non-monotonic wiggles, or a local non-convexity that no human would have written down.

I'd hold two views at once.

The first is the skeptical one. Some of that structure could be an artifact. The meta-optimizer is overfitting to the training distribution of tasks, exploiting a quirk of the inner-loop optimizer, or just carrying noise in a region where the function has little effect on the outcome. If the gradient signal there doesn't matter much, the search has no pressure to make it clean. So "the algorithm found it" isn't automatically "this is deep truth." You have to ablate it: remove the feature, smooth it out, and see whether performance drops, and whether that holds when you transfer to held-out tasks.

The second view is the exciting one. The region around zero advantage and zero deviation is exactly where most of the data lives during training. Most samples are close to on-policy, and most advantages are small and noisy. So if anywhere is going to reward sophisticated shaping, it's there. A feature that, say, slightly pushes you away from the current policy when the signal is ambiguous could be acting as implicit exploration. Or it could be a regularizer that keeps you from collapsing too early onto noisy preference signal. In the preference setting, the mix of a logistic-style loss and an exponential-style loss we saw has this flavor: different behavior depending on how confident you already are. That's plausibly a real inductive bias that we humans just haven't articulated.

To me, the methodological point is that these discovered functions are hypothesis generators, not final answers. The workflow I like is: discover, find the surprising bit, then try to explain it with theory or a targeted experiment, and only then believe it. Sometimes the explanation gives you a new principled algorithm, and sometimes you conclude it was a quirk. Both outcomes are useful. What I don't want is people treating a meta-learned black box as an oracle, or dismissing the weird bits as noise without checking.

So the honest answer is that those higher-order features are currently open questions. That's what makes this kind of automated discovery fun. It points our attention at the parts of algorithm space where our intuitions are weakest.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether the near-origin features matter, suggesting they may be artifacts with little effect and recommending ablations to check whether removing or smoothing them reduces performance.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something that I find genuinely fascinating, and I think it gets at a deeper point about how we should think about these methods. If you look at DPO, the headline story is quite clean, right? You take the RLHF objective, you solve for the optimal policy in closed form under the KL constraint, you substitute that back in, and you get this nice supervised classification loss on preference pairs. No reward model, no sampling, no PPO machinery. And that's a beautiful derivation.

But what happens when you actually analyze the gradient is that you find structure that the derivation doesn't obviously tell you to expect. Around the point where you have zero advantage, where the chosen and rejected completions are essentially tied in implicit reward, and where you have zero deviation from the reference policy, so the policy hasn't moved yet, the loss landscape has this curvature and these interaction terms that look like higher-order corrections you'd normally only see if you expanded the KL penalty out to second order or beyond. And people have noticed that DPO behaves in ways you wouldn't predict from a naive first-order picture. Likelihood of both chosen and rejected goes down, the policy drifts off the data manifold, you get these displacement effects.

My view is that these features are not accidents, and they're not bugs in the usual sense. They're telling you that the mapping from the RL objective to the supervised objective hides a lot in the reparameterization. When you eliminate the reward model, you don't eliminate the dynamics of the reward model, you fold them into the policy's logits. So the thing that would have been exploration or reward hacking in a PPO setup now shows up as weird geometry in the preference loss. The zero-advantage, zero-deviation point is exactly where the implicit reward is most degenerate, so you're essentially sitting at a saddle, and the higher-order terms are what decide which direction you fall.

Coming from a multi-agent and game theory background, I actually think this is a familiar story. In learning in games, you spend a lot of time around fixed points where the first-order signal vanishes and all the interesting behavior, convergence, cycling, divergence, is governed by second-order structure. DPO is a two-player game in disguise. The chosen and rejected completions are, in a sense, adversaries, and the reference policy is a regularizer that's pinning you to a particular equilibrium. So the fact that you get unexplained curvature at the equilibrium point is, to me, the least surprising thing in the world. What's surprising is that the community was initially a bit surprised by it.

The practical upshot is that I think we should stop treating DPO as "RLHF but simpler" and start treating it as its own optimization problem with its own failure modes. Things like IPO, or the various length-regularized variants, or adding an SFT term, these are all attempts to explicitly handle the higher-order behavior that the original derivation swept under the rug. And I'd argue the right research direction isn't to patch it empirically but to actually characterize those terms. If you understand why the gradient does what it does at the degenerate point, you can design the regularizer from first principles rather than by trial and error.

So, in short, I view them as the cost of the closed-form shortcut. You got rid of the explicit RL loop, but the RL didn't go away, it just became implicit, and the higher-order features are where it's showing through.

r001.rationale: The response says the higher-order features are not accidents and affect DPO’s behavior, citing likelihood decreases, policy drift, and optimization failure modes.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re interesting, but I don’t think we have a good explanation for them yet. Around zero advantage and zero deviation from the policy, you can look at the local structure and ask what those higher-order terms are doing. But identifying that structure isn’t the same as understanding why it helps.

I’d treat them as hypotheses to investigate. You’d want to remove or modify those terms, see whether the performance changes, and check whether the effect persists across settings. Until then, I wouldn’t attach too strong a mechanistic interpretation to them.

r001.rationale: The response treats the features’ effect as unestablished and proposes removing or modifying them to see whether performance changes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we don’t yet have a good explanation for them. Around zero advantage and zero deviation from the policy, you can look at a local expansion and understand some of the leading-order behavior. But that doesn’t tell you why these particular higher-order terms appear, or whether they’re actually responsible for the improvement.

One possibility is that they shape the optimization as you move away from that local regime. But I’d treat that as a hypothesis. You’d want to ablate those terms, see which ones matter, and check whether the effect persists across environments and training runs. Until then, they’re an interesting empirical finding rather than something I’d claim we understand.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether the higher-order terms are responsible for improvement and proposes ablations to check whether they matter, directly questioning their functional effect.
